quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Supermarkets are arranged with care. Milk and bread are often placed at the back, so shoppers walk past shelves of tempting snacks on the way. Sweets appear near the checkout, where waiting customers have time to look. None of this is accidental: stores test different layouts and keep the ones that lead to larger purchases.
options: How Store Layouts Steer What Shoppers Buy
Why Milk Is Kept at the Back
quests.correctAnswer: How Store Layouts Steer What Shoppers Buy
quests.hint: The examples are about where things sit. What is the writer using them to show?
quests.explanation: Milk at the back and sweets at the checkout are two examples of one strategy. The final sentence states the purpose behind all placements.
quests.whyThisTitle: Both placements and the store testing show that layout is designed to influence purchases.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On a busy highway in the mountains, engineers built a wide, grass-covered bridge for animals. Deer, foxes, and even bears use it to cross safely. Since it opened, collisions with wildlife have fallen sharply, and fewer drivers have been hurt. The cost was high, but officials say the project has paid for itself in repair bills and hospital costs saved.
options: Why Highways Harm Nature and Wildlife Habitats
The High Cost of Building Bridges Over Highways
Protecting Animals and Drivers with a Bridge
quests.correctAnswer: Protecting Animals and Drivers with a Bridge
quests.hint: Who benefits from the bridge? Check whether a title mentions all of them.
quests.explanation: The cost and the bears are single details, and highways harming nature is a much bigger topic. The bridge helps two groups, and that is what the passage develops.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice reflects both the animals' safe crossing and the drop in accidents for drivers.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Tomas plays the accordion outside the central station every evening. Most commuters hurry past, but a few slow down, and some drop coins into the open case. He says the money is not the reason he comes. Playing among strangers taught him to keep going even when nobody seems to listen, and that has helped him in his job as a salesman.
options: Earning Extra Money as a Street Musician
quests.correctAnswer: Lessons from a Street Corner
quests.hint: Tomas himself tells you what matters to him. What is it?
quests.explanation: Coins and hurried commuters are part of the scene, but Tomas says they are not the point. The passage is about what he learned and how it helps him at work.
quests.whyThisTitle: The music matters because the experience taught him to keep going, which he applies to selling.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: At the monthly repair café, people bring broken toasters, torn jackets, and wobbly chairs. Volunteers with tools and patience help visitors fix things themselves, rather than doing it for them. Coffee is free, and conversation is half the fun. Organizers hope the event will teach people that many objects worth keeping can be mended cheaply.
options: Why People Buy So Many Gadgets
How to Choose the Right Tools for Home Repairs
Mending and Learning at a Neighborhood Event
quests.correctAnswer: Mending and Learning at a Neighborhood Event
quests.hint: Look at what volunteers do: they help people do something themselves. What does the event give people?
quests.explanation: The coffee and the tools are supporting details. The event exists so that people can repair things and learn how, which the title reflects.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title joins the mending of objects with the learning that volunteers encourage.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Freelancers who work from home often miss the presence of others. A shared workspace offers desks, fast internet, and a coffee machine for a monthly fee. Many members say the biggest benefit is not the equipment but the chance conversations: a designer meets a developer, and a new project begins.
options: Freelancers and the Appeal of Shared Workspaces
How Designers and Developers Collaborate on Projects
quests.correctAnswer: Freelancers and the Appeal of Shared Workspaces
quests.hint: Ask what members say matters most. Is it the equipment, or something else?
quests.explanation: Internet and desks are the obvious features, but the passage says the real value lies elsewhere. The title must explain why people choose these spaces, not just what they contain.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the reason members give: contact with other professionals as well as a place to work.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A small wooden box stands at the end of Cedar Lane. Anyone may take a book from it or leave one behind. It began as a school project, but now neighbors keep it stocked with novels, cookbooks, and children's stories. Its popularity has inspired three more boxes in the district.
options: Neighborhood Book Box Catches On with Residents
Building Wooden Boxes as a School Project
How to Choose Stories for Children
quests.correctAnswer: Neighborhood Book Box Catches On with Residents
quests.hint: Follow the story from beginning to end: what starts small and then grows?
quests.explanation: The school project is only how it began. The passage traces how one box spread in popularity.
quests.whyThisTitle: The take-or-leave system and the three new boxes show a simple idea gaining a following.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In small towns, many firefighters have other jobs. When the alarm sounds, a baker leaves the oven and a teacher leaves the classroom. They train together twice a month and often give up weekends for extra practice. Residents rely on them, and they rely on each other.
options: Training Together Twice a Month on Weekends
Leaving Work When the Alarm Sounds
quests.correctAnswer: Neighbors Who Serve as Firefighters
quests.hint: Look at the people described in the first two sentences. Who are they?
quests.explanation: Training and leaving work are details about how these people serve. The title should say who they are and what role they play.
quests.whyThisTitle: The baker and the teacher illustrate residents with regular jobs who also serve as firefighters.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Night classes at the community college attract more than teenagers. This term, a bus driver is learning accounting, a grandmother is studying computer skills, and a young father is finishing a high-school diploma. Some hope for a promotion; others just want to prove something to themselves. The classroom is full of tired but determined faces.
quests.correctAnswer: Grown-Ups Back in the Classroom
quests.hint: The three students are examples. What do their stories show as a group?
quests.explanation: Accounting and promotions are single examples. The passage places several different learners side by side to show a wider pattern.
quests.whyThisTitle: The bus driver, the grandmother, and the father illustrate the variety of adults and motives.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Before winter, mechanics recommend checking the battery, because cold weather makes it lose strength. Tires should have enough tread to grip icy roads, and the windshield fluid should be a type that will not freeze. It is also wise to keep a blanket and a flashlight in the trunk. Most winter breakdowns can be avoided with an hour of preparation.
options: Preparing Your Car for Safe Winter Driving
Driving Carefully on Icy Winter Roads
quests.correctAnswer: Preparing Your Car for Safe Winter Driving
quests.hint: Notice that the final sentence sums up everything before it.
quests.explanation: The battery, the trunk items, and the tires are all separate checks. Driving on ice would require advice about behavior, which the passage never gives.
quests.whyThisTitle: Each recommendation is a step in getting the car ready before winter arrives.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In the city's train stations, signs appear in three languages. The change began after visitors from abroad reported getting lost. Some residents worried that the signs would clutter the walls, but designers used larger symbols and clearer colors. Now travelers find platforms faster, and locals say the stations feel more welcoming.
quests.correctAnswer: Signs That Guide Travelers
quests.hint: There was a worry and a solution. Which title includes the result that matters most?
quests.explanation: Clutter and color choices are parts of the process. The passage concludes that the signs work for visitors and locals alike.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers the reason for the new signs and the improved experience for both travelers and residents.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When a forecast says there is a forty percent chance of rain, many people think it will rain for forty percent of the day. In fact, the number describes how likely it is that rain will fall somewhere in the forecast area. A high number does not mean heavy rain, and a low number does not rule out a storm. Reading the percentage correctly helps people decide whether to bring an umbrella.
options: Deciding Whether to Carry an Umbrella
Reading a Rain Forecast Percentage Correctly
quests.correctAnswer: Reading a Rain Forecast Percentage Correctly
quests.hint: Ask what mistake the passage is correcting.
quests.explanation: The umbrella is the practical use, and the prediction methods are not covered. The passage clears up a common misunderstanding of the number.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title targets the misreading the passage explains, from time of rain to likelihood of rain.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Nine-year-old Ruby set up a lemonade stand and sold cups for a dollar. After an hour, she noticed that she had spent more on lemons and sugar than she had earned. Her father suggested she count each cost. When she raised the price and used fewer lemons, she finally made a small profit, and she learned that a busy stand is not always a successful one.
options: Ruby's Lemonade Stand and a Lesson in Profit
Buying Lemons and Sugar in Bulk
Why Children Enjoy Selling Things to Neighbors
Setting Prices for a Big Store
quests.correctAnswer: Ruby's Lemonade Stand and a Lesson in Profit
quests.hint: The final clause states what Ruby understood by the end. Which title matches that?
quests.explanation: Costs and prices are steps along the way. The story exists to show what Ruby understood by the end.
quests.whyThisTitle: The costs, the price rise, and her conclusion all lead to the idea of profit.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: If your suitcase does not appear on the belt, go to the baggage desk before leaving the airport. Staff will ask for your claim tag and a description of the bag, then enter it into a tracking system. Most delayed bags arrive within two days, and the airline will deliver them to your address. Keep your receipts if you buy essentials, since some airlines repay reasonable costs.
options: Steps to Take for Missing Luggage
Why Suitcases Are Lost in Transit
quests.correctAnswer: Steps to Take for Missing Luggage
quests.hint: Think about who the reader is and what they need in this situation.
quests.explanation: Tracking and receipts are individual steps. The passage guides a traveler through the whole situation, and it does not explain causes.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice matches the steps advised from reporting the loss to recovering costs.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On the roof of a downtown hotel, four beehives produce honey for the restaurant below. Bees fly up to three kilometers to visit gardens and parks, so the honey tastes of the city's flowers. The chef uses it in desserts and drinks. Guests can join a tour, wear protective suits, and watch the keeper at work.
options: Wearing Protective Suits on Bee Tours
The Decline of Wild Bees Worldwide
quests.correctAnswer: Bees Supplying a Hotel Kitchen
quests.hint: Which title covers where the bees are kept and where the honey goes?
quests.explanation: Desserts and tours are details along the chain. The passage links rooftop hives to the hotel's restaurant.
quests.whyThisTitle: The hives, the flavor of local flowers, and the chef's use all connect to the hotel kitchen.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Cities that add public drinking fountains often see fewer plastic bottles in the trash. But fountains only work if people know where they are. Some cities now show their locations on tourist maps and phone apps. Others paint the fountains bright colors so they are easy to spot from a distance.
options: Painting City Fountains in Bright Colors
quests.correctAnswer: Helping People Find Water Fountains
quests.hint: Look at the word 'but.' What problem does it introduce?
quests.explanation: Fewer bottles is the goal, and painting and maps are two solutions. The passage's focus is visibility.
quests.whyThisTitle: After naming the benefit, the passage turns to the problem of visibility and how cities respond.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A board game café gives customers a library of games to play while they eat. Staff members act as guides, teaching rules so nobody has to read a thick manual. Many guests arrive as strangers and leave as friends, since games give people something to talk about besides work. The cafés charge an entry fee instead of selling games.
options: Why Board Games Are So Expensive to Buy
quests.correctAnswer: Café Built Around Playing Together
quests.hint: Ask what the café offers that a normal café does not.
quests.explanation: The fee and the staff's role are features that make the idea work. The passage describes a café whose main activity is shared play.
quests.whyThisTitle: The games, the guides, and the friendships all support the idea of a café for playing together.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A group of retirees in their seventies meets each Wednesday for a ride along the canal. They keep a slow pace and stop at a café halfway. One member began cycling after his doctor suggested more exercise, but he says the friendships keep him coming back. Others agree that the group gives their week a shape.
options: A Guide to Choosing a Café for a Rest Stop
Following a Doctor's Advice on Exercise
More Than Exercise for Senior Cyclists
quests.correctAnswer: More Than Exercise for Senior Cyclists
quests.hint: One member says why he keeps coming. What does that suggest about the group?
quests.explanation: Exercise is why one member began, but the passage stresses the friendships. The title must show the club has more to offer than riding.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title acknowledges the cycling and the friendship the members say matter most.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Hotel cleaners often follow strict routines: strip the bed, check the bathroom, restock supplies, and vacuum. A single room may take half an hour, and a cleaner might handle fifteen rooms a day. Yet guests rarely see them at work. Managers say the reputation of a hotel depends on the small details these staff check, like whether a lamp works or a towel is missing.
options: Cleaning Fifteen Hotel Rooms in a Single Day
How Small Checks Shape a Hotel's Name
quests.correctAnswer: How Small Checks Shape a Hotel's Name
quests.hint: The final sentence gives the managers' view. How does it change what the earlier facts mean?
quests.explanation: The workload facts describe the job. The last sentence explains why that work matters, which is the writer's real point.
quests.whyThisTitle: The routines and room counts matter because the small checks shape how guests judge the hotel.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The town's radio station has three paid staff and sixty volunteers. Retired teachers read the news, teenagers present music shows, and a farmer reports the price of grain each morning. Although the station cannot compete with big broadcasters, listeners say it is the only place where they hear their own neighbors' voices.
options: Farmers Reporting Grain Prices Each Morning
Why a Local Radio Station Matters
quests.correctAnswer: Why a Local Radio Station Matters
quests.hint: Look for the point after 'although.'
quests.explanation: The farmer and teenagers are examples of who takes part. The final sentence tells you why listeners value the station.
quests.whyThisTitle: The volunteers' variety supports the claim that listeners hear their own community on air.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: At a job fair, most applicants bring their résumé and hope for the best. The ones who stand out do research beforehand, learn what each company does, and prepare a question for the recruiter. A short, specific question shows interest and gets remembered. Recruiters say they meet hundreds of people in a day, and only a few make a lasting impression.
options: How Recruiters Meet Hundreds of People
quests.correctAnswer: Standing Out at Job Fairs
quests.hint: Compare what most applicants do with what the memorable ones do.
quests.explanation: Research and the recruiter's workload are parts of the argument. The passage's point is how to be remembered.
quests.whyThisTitle: The preparation and the specific question are both ways of making an impression.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The pedestrian tunnel under Station Road used to be dark and unpleasant. Last summer, local artists and students painted it with scenes of the neighborhood's history. Now people walk through more willingly, and reports of littering have dropped. The council is asking other communities to consider similar projects.
options: Why Councils Choose to Fund Public Art
The Change a Painted Tunnel Brought
quests.correctAnswer: The Change a Painted Tunnel Brought
quests.hint: Which title includes both the painting and its effects?
quests.explanation: Litter reduction is one effect, and funding is only hinted at. The passage tells how a tunnel changed after it was painted.
quests.whyThisTitle: It links the artists' work to the changed behavior of residents.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When Leo hosted an exchange student from Chile, he expected to teach her about local life. Instead, she introduced him to new foods and asked questions he had never considered. By the end of the year, he realized he had learned as much as he had taught. Leo now says hosting changed how he sees his own town.
options: Preparing to Host a Student from Abroad
Learning from an Exchange Student in His Home
quests.correctAnswer: Learning from an Exchange Student in His Home
quests.hint: Ask how Leo's expectation at the beginning differs from what he found.
quests.explanation: The foods and the hosting preparation are details. The passage turns on a reversal: the host became the learner.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the reversal from teaching to learning that the passage builds toward.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many restaurants now print photos beside each dish on their menus. Diners who cannot read the language can simply point, and staff avoid long explanations. Some chefs worry that photos make a place look less refined. Owners, however, report fewer mistakes with orders and shorter waits at busy hours.
options: Pointing to Dishes as a Tourist
quests.correctAnswer: Restaurants Adding Photos to Menus
quests.hint: The passage includes an objection and a reply. Which title reflects the reply?
quests.explanation: Refinement is the chefs' concern, and pointing is one benefit. The passage explains the practical reasons owners choose photos.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title matches the owners' reasons: easier ordering, fewer errors, and shorter waits.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Rain is rare in the desert town of Marsa, but when it falls, the streets turn into rivers within minutes. Residents keep sandbags by their doors and listen for warnings. Children run outside to watch, while shopkeepers hurry to move goods off the floor. Afterward, the dry ground blooms with small green plants that last only a few weeks.
options: Living Through Rare Rain in a Desert Town
Warnings About Sudden Floods in Large Cities
quests.correctAnswer: Living Through Rare Rain in a Desert Town
quests.hint: Ask what the whole town does, from the warning to the aftermath.
quests.explanation: Sandbags and blooming are single moments. The passage follows the town's response to rain from start to finish.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice joins the preparation, the flood, and the aftermath as one experience of the town.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Hospital designers now pay attention to waiting rooms. Soft lighting, comfortable seats, and views of trees can reduce visitors' anxiety. Some hospitals add quiet play areas for children and charging points for phones. Studies show that patients who feel calm before an appointment communicate more clearly with doctors.
options: Waiting Rooms That Calm Anxious Patients
How Doctors Talk to Patients Clearly
quests.correctAnswer: Waiting Rooms That Calm Anxious Patients
quests.hint: Look at the reason given for the design changes.
quests.explanation: Phone chargers are one feature, and doctor communication is one benefit. Every feature and the study serve the goal of calming patients.
quests.whyThisTitle: Every feature named is meant to reduce anxiety, which the study says helps communication.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many taxi drivers complained when navigation apps became common, fearing that passengers would no longer need their knowledge. Yet some drivers report the opposite. Passengers trust the app for directions but still ask drivers about traffic, shortcuts, and safe areas. The best drivers now use the app to save time and their own experience to make good decisions.
quests.correctAnswer: Taxi Drivers and Navigation Apps
quests.hint: Look at how the drivers' view changes over the passage.
quests.explanation: The complaints are only the starting point. The passage moves toward how drivers combine the app with their own knowledge.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the fears at the start and the partnership between app and driver at the end.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Long flights are easier when you plan how to sleep. A neck pillow keeps your head steady, and an eye mask blocks cabin lights. Choosing a window seat means no one needs to climb over you. Some travelers set their watch to the destination's time as soon as they board, so their body begins adjusting to the new schedule.
options: Why Jet Lag Is So Difficult
Setting Your Watch to a New Time Zone
quests.correctAnswer: Making Long Flights More Restful
quests.hint: Count the different tips. What goal do they share?
quests.explanation: Seat choice and watch setting are two tips among several, and the causes of jet lag are not explained. The passage is about resting better in flight.
quests.whyThisTitle: The pillow, mask, seat, and watch trick all serve the aim of sleeping well on a long flight.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Referees are noticed most when they make mistakes. A good game often goes by without anyone remembering the person in the middle. Yet the job requires constant judgment, quick decisions, and staying calm while thousands of people shout. Many referees begin as teenagers, and they learn to accept criticism as part of the work.
options: The Thankless Job of a Sports Referee
Why Fans Shout at Games They Care About
quests.correctAnswer: The Thankless Job of a Sports Referee
quests.hint: Which idea appears in both the first two sentences and the last?
quests.explanation: Starting as teenagers and crowd noise are pieces of context. The passage keeps returning to how little credit referees receive.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the passage's theme that good refereeing is invisible and criticism is expected.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Since her grandmother's death, Amira has been trying to recreate her stew. There was no written recipe, only memories of smell and a habit of adding spices by handfuls. Amira asked aunts and cousins, and each remembered a different ingredient. After a dozen attempts, the taste is close, and the search has brought the family together more than the meal itself.
options: The Recipe That Reunited a Family
quests.correctAnswer: The Recipe That Reunited a Family
quests.hint: The last clause says the search mattered more than the meal. What does that suggest?
quests.explanation: The spices and the grandmother's death are background. The passage's real subject is what the search produced among relatives.
quests.whyThisTitle: The relatives' shared memories, not the finished stew, are the passage's outcome.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Long before dawn, the harbor market is loud with shouting. Fishermen unload crates of ice and silver fish, and buyers move quickly from stall to stall, judging freshness by eye and smell. Deals are made in minutes. By seven o'clock, most of the catch is sold, and the workers hose down the floor for the next day.
options: The Hard Life of a Harbor Fisherman
Morning Rush at the Fish Market
quests.correctAnswer: Morning Rush at the Fish Market
quests.hint: Ask what time span and what kind of pace the passage describes.
quests.explanation: Judging by smell and hosing down the floor are moments inside a longer scene. The passage describes the whole busy morning.
quests.whyThisTitle: From the shouting before dawn to the cleaning at seven, everything happens in one hurried morning.
